blocks.content: A message queue is a concrete, kernel provided implementation of the message passing model covered in the previous chapter, specifically built to solve two things a plain pipe cannot: preserving distinct message boundaries, and letting messages be tagged with a type so a reader can selectively pick which ones to receive.

This chapter treats message queues as the natural next step after both pipes and the general message passing model, showing concretely how a real kernel object fills in the indirect naming and structured message ideas introduced generally in the previous chapter.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507303-391987325.png
1. The Core Problem a Message Queue Solves
blocks.text: 1. The Core Problem a Message Queue Solves

blocks.content: The pipes chapter was explicit that a pipe moves a raw, unstructured stream of bytes, with no concept of a message boundary built in at all. If one process writes three separate logical messages into a pipe back to back, the reading process has no built in way to know where one message ends and the next begins, that structure has to be layered on manually by the application itself.

A message queue fixes this directly by making the message the fundamental unit of the channel, not the byte. Every message sent onto a queue is received as one complete, discrete unit, exactly as it was sent, with the kernel itself preserving that boundary, no manual framing required by the application.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507304-931552451.png
blocks.alt: The Core Problem a Message Queue Solves

blocks.content: 2. Typed Messages: Selective Receiving

Beyond simply preserving boundaries, a message queue lets every message carry an integer type tag alongside its actual payload. A single shared queue can hold messages of several different types all mixed together, and critically, a receiving process can choose to receive only messages of a specific type, skipping past the others entirely.

This directly implements the indirect naming idea from the message passing chapter in a genuinely useful, concrete way: multiple logically distinct conversations can share one physical queue, distinguished purely by their type tag, rather than needing a completely separate queue for every distinct kind of message.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507304-254532432.png

3. Persistence: Outliving the Processes That Use It
blocks.text: 3. Persistence: Outliving the Processes That Use It

blocks.content: A pipe, the pipes chapter was clear about this, exists only as long as both its ends stay open, it is tightly bound to the lifetime of the processes using it. A message queue is fundamentally different: it is a genuine kernel object with its own independent identity, created with a specific key, that persists in the kernel regardless of whether any process is currently using it.

This means a message queue can hold undelivered messages even while no process is actively reading from it, and can be reopened later by an entirely different process using the same key, a real, practical form of loose coupling between producers and consumers that do not need to be running at the exact same time.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507304-135410375.png
blocks.alt: Persistence: Outliving the Processes That Use It

blocks.title: A real consequence worth knowing
blocks.content: Because a message queue persists independently, it must also be explicitly removed, it is not automatically cleaned up just because the processes using it have exited, exactly the same kind of explicit cleanup responsibility the shared memory chapter described for shared memory segments.
4. Multiple Writers and Readers

A single message queue can have multiple processes writing onto it and multiple processes reading from it simultaneously, unlike a typical pipe which usually connects one writer to one reader. Each individual message, though, is still delivered to exactly one reader, not broadcast to every reader listening on the queue.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507612-534702053.png
5. The Core API

The classic System V message queue API on Unix like systems follows a small, consistent set of operations. msgget creates a new queue or opens an existing one identified by a specific key. msgsnd sends a typed message onto the queue. msgrcv receives a message, optionally filtering by a specific type. msgctl with the IPC_RMID flag explicitly removes the queue entirely.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507613-84693879.png
6. A Practical Use Case: Distributing Work Across Workers
blocks.text: 6. A Practical Use Case: Distributing Work Across Workers

blocks.content: A very common real world pattern is a single producer process placing tasks onto a shared message queue, with a pool of worker processes each reading from that same queue, each task delivered to whichever worker happens to be ready next. This is a natural, kernel provided way to build a task distribution system without any custom coordination logic.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507613-191033683.png
blocks.alt: A Practical Use Case: Distributing Work Across Workers

7. Cleanup Is a Real Responsibility

Because a message queue persists independently of any process using it, forgetting to remove it explicitly leaves it lingering indefinitely as a real kernel resource, exactly the same leaked resource risk the shared memory chapter warned about for shared memory segments left undetached and unremoved.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507613-312109401.png
8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming a message queue works like a pipe with no real structural difference, when preserving discrete message boundaries and supporting typed, selective receiving are the two features specifically distinguishing it from a plain pipe.","Forgetting that a message queue is a persistent kernel object that must be explicitly removed, unlike a pipe which naturally disappears once both ends are closed.","Assuming a message sent onto a queue with multiple readers gets delivered to all of them, when each individual message is still consumed by exactly one reader."]
items: Assuming a message queue works like a pipe with no real structural difference, when preserving discrete message boundaries and supporting typed, selective receiving are the two features specifically distinguishing it from a plain pipe.
Forgetting that a message queue is a persistent kernel object that must be explicitly removed, unlike a pipe which naturally disappears once both ends are closed.
Assuming a message sent onto a queue with multiple readers gets delivered to all of them, when each individual message is still consumed by exactly one reader.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain precisely what a message queue offers that a plain pipe does not, message boundaries and typed selective receiving, and to connect its persistence and explicit cleanup requirement directly back to the same theme already covered for shared memory segments.

Message queues show one concrete, structured implementation of the message passing model. The next chapter covers sockets, the mechanism that extends this same general model across an actual network, not just within one machine.
